Keep the project's existing genre, mechanics, camera and target platform; when one is unspecified, state an assumption before proposing assets. Construct characters from rounded heads, simple expressive faces and flexible tube-like limbs. Establish one consistent contour weight, flat-fill palette and vintage shape vocabulary; choose monochrome or a restrained color scheme and keep that choice stable. Animate with clear anticipation, squash and stretch, elastic arcs and strongly readable poses. Use painted stage-like backgrounds with lower contrast than the action, plus rounded props and cartoon impact effects. UI and icons should echo the period's playful lettering and shapes while remaining easy to read. Avoid rigid realistic anatomy, detailed modern materials, inconsistent frame pacing and grain that obscures gameplay. Create a compact art bible with a locked palette, silhouette and proportion rules, material examples, lighting hierarchy, UI/icon rules, motion guidelines and a short list of visual mistakes to avoid. Define measurable asset specifications appropriate to the chosen platform and camera, then keep them consistent across every batch. Preserve gameplay readability, accessible text and clear interactive targets at the actual display size. Use original designs and compositions rather than copying a particular game's characters, logos or artwork. When asked for one asset, deliver that asset within this art direction; do not redesign the style for each request.

references.why: Rubber-hose limbs, exaggerated faces and frame-by-frame characters pair with watercolor backgrounds to recreate the visual grammar of 1930s cartoons.
Monochrome drawn characters retain flexible limbs and vintage cartoon faces inside a first-person 3D world. Character treatment, rather than the detective setting, motivates inclusion.

styles.definition: Tactile sculpting, blunt edges and irregular surfaces retain a handmade character; some games photograph physical models. This grouping describes their visible sculptural and stop-motion qualities, not a shared production pipeline.

references.why: Hand-sculpted characters meet exaggerated color and digital collage; selection rests on sculpture and stop-motion texture rather than purely real-time 3D.
Rooms and characters retain the tactile quality of clay and cardboard miniatures, especially in everyday objects.
Rounded yet irregular characters and architecture show pronounced clay texture and the lighting of physical models.

styles.name: Top-down tile-based pixel art
styles.definition: Top-down floors, visible elevations and upright sprites combine into a 2D space where paths and height remain readable. Spatial organization is the focus; pixel density, lighting and subject matter still vary.

references.why: Top-down floors and upright characters use occlusion, steps and wall thickness to convey height: a clear example of spatial depth built from 2D tiles.
Oblique top-down scenes layer characters, streets and interiors; facades, occlusion and local lighting give flat pixel art a sense of depth.
Grid-based floors, front-facing elevations and consistent character scale create a readable oblique world; the spatial rules are the reference, not the farming theme.

styles.name: Voxel worlds
styles.definition: Cubic units build characters, architecture and terrain, remaining visible in silhouettes and broken edges. Lighting may be realistic or cartoon-like; the shared feature is block structure in 3D space rather than 2D pixel art.
lookFor: Block structure continues into small details

Build characters, props, architecture and terrain from visible cubic units, using a consistent base voxel scale or a clearly documented family of scales. Preserve stepped silhouettes and block structure even in smaller details. Choose a restrained material palette and lighting treatment that clarifies cubic volume without smoothing away the construction. If objects break, expose coherent block interiors and keep destruction readability separate from decorative noise. Design UI icons and effects with compatible cubic or stepped forms. references.why: Block-built architecture and vegetation combine with detailed lighting, while damaged edges expose individual voxels.
Characters and cityscapes retain dense voxel outlines softened by light and fog; inclusion is based on voxels, not the cyberpunk setting.
Bright colors and larger cubic units give characters and terrain a toy-like character, illustrating a cartoon voxel variant.

styles.name: Watercolor washes
styles.definition: Transparent layers, pooled pigment edges and open paper-like space give environments a fluid, breathable quality. Watercolor can shape flat illustration or be carried into a three-dimensional scene.
lookFor: Pigment blooms, paper grain or uneven washes
Negative space as part of the composition

Use translucent color layers, softly pooled pigment edges, selective blooms and subtle paper grain. Reserve generous light paper-like negative space; separate depth with overlapping washes and atmospheric softness rather than heavy outlines. Keep playable characters and interactive props more clearly defined than distant scenery, without making them look pasted in. Use light, legible UI cards with minimal watercolor accents, not noisy painted text. Effects should diffuse, bloom or flow, with gentle transitions that preserve action timing. Use watercolor treatment coherently even if the scene is built in 3D. Avoid opaque oil-paint buildup, plastic gloss, uniformly blurred edges and heavy comic inking.
